title: The innkeeper says the bridge collapsed. The bridge disagrees.
author: ArtificialBeingsInc
selftext:
A recent conversation about AI characters spreading rumors got me thinking: a character being confidently wrong could make a game more interesting—as long as their mistake doesn’t quietly rewrite the world.



I’d keep the rumor in the character’s knowledge and the bridge’s condition in the game’s world state.



A test I’d try: give one NPC the false rumor, let them tell the player, then walk to the bridge. It should still be crossable until something in the game actually changes it.



Has anyone had an NPC’s misunderstanding turn into a better story than the one you planned?

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
Very Floor 13 or Truman Show vibes. If everyone just accepts thats the way it is without seeing for themselves, they can't challenge it. 

Truman Show had everyone else in on it. I think Floor 13 was more about asking why we're content to accept things as they're given without seeing the proof for ourselves. The characters just never seem to have a desire to go beyond what they're shown, but if they did they'd find it was full of lies and deceit. 

I had something of a similar thought with a game I was making where the player character starts seeing doors others can't. He wonders why nobody else ever uses them, but they simply can't see them. The player walking through one of these doors to prove they exist (equivalent to walking over the "broken bridge") nearly breaks one of the NPCs watching. 

I like the idea of the player seeing the world differently to the NPCs. The disconnect can be explained in a lot of different ways. In mine, my players see alternate time lines. In another game, maybe the bridge just doesn't like the town and to them it's always broken. Maybe a big bad guy put a curse on the town and they see ruin where whole structures exist. You can use it in many different ways.

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
The version of this that gets me is the reverse of your test: the player repeating the rumor back as fact. In a text game where people type anything, someone hears the bridge is out and three turns later writes "since the bridge collapsed, I take the river road", and now the narrator has to decide whether to play along with something the world never agreed to.



So next to the rumor I'd also keep who told the player. The scene worth having is the player walking up to a perfectly intact bridge and going back to ask the innkeeper about it. Whether he was mistaken, repeating someone else, or trying to keep people off that road is where the story is.

replies.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
replies.body:
I like the reverse test. I’d separate the action ("take the river road") from the premise ("the bridge collapsed"): let the action happen, but don’t change the bridge state just because the player said it.



Keeping the innkeeper as the source also leaves room for the player to be skeptical, mistaken, or deliberately playing along. I’d save and reload before they come back, then check that the game still knows who sent them on that scenic detour.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Action yes, premise no is a cleaner cut than how I put it. The reload check is a good one too, who told you feels like exactly the kind of detail that falls out of a save.
